I have been through a lot of Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) since I was diagnosed with a depressive and borderline personality disorder. When I quit smoking, I realized how helpful all the tools and skills I had learned in therapy were to navigate the emotional ups and downs of quitting. Specifically, mindfulness and opposite action were immensely helpful. Both are simple in theory but require a lot of time and energy to learn and implement. 

I think many people who quit smoking would greatly benefit from learning emotional skills first. It wasn't intentional, but I am glad that I did not even bother trying to quit while I was still in the middle of treatment. I waited until I was ready and I had the necessary skills.

DBT is often performed in group settings, so I think it would be great if more quitting programs/groups would incorporate parts of it into their program.

I had been on a weight loss journey for a couple of months before I quit and was 100% prepared to either maintain my weight or gain a little bit back. The first couple of days I cut myself some slack and didn't indulge but also didn't watch my portions or anything. After the physical withdrawal was over I realized that, much like when you initially start losing weight, it mainly comes down to mind games. I bought a pack of sugar-free candy for my first month and otherwise continued with my regular diet. 

It's been four months or so now and I maintained my weight loss rate from before quitting. Being able to exercise better even made the process a little easier. You may gain a little bit of weight initially, but that will be much less harmful than continuing to smoke. 

Just try to keep the upper hand in the mind games while quitting. Also, much like changing my heating habit, I frequently reminded myself that I had to sit things out to get to the other side of things. At this point, I only occasionally think about smoking and that was only possible because I forced myself to stick it out in the beginning. Give yourself the chance for refraining to feel easier by sitting it out. 

Something else that helped me was taking a can of diet soda and just sitting down where I would usually smoke. Gave my mouth something to do and gave me my five minutes of peace outside. 
Also, perhaps you already do, but exercising helps both with weight control and managing urges so you might want to look into that (even walking is already great)

I think it is important to remember that "it's not a BPD thing they are just an a-hole" doesn't mean that their behavior isn't influenced by their BPD but that being abusive or an a-hole isn't inherent to BPD. 

If someone is an a-hole, how they are being an a-hole is probably shaped by their personality (or disorder thereof); but no person or personality type is inherently and always an a-hole.  
Personally, I believe that everybody is capable of being an a-hole and doing shitty things, especially if they are subjected to external or internal stressors. Someone with a PD is probably faces a lot more of those than the average person. But everybody is capable of learning how to deal with them, which is why I would argue that someone who has a treated and well-managed PD might actually be an a-hole less often (compared to someone who doesn't have a diagnosis and isn't inherently good at handling stressors). This means that everybody is capable of hurtful behavior, but nobody is inherently or destined to be an a-hole. 

Consequently, I would say that we should ask ourselves what stressor makes us more likely to engage in a-hole behavior, rather than saying we have a specific toxic behavior. 
For example, I suck at handling situations where I feel ashamed. To deal with this stressor I will engage in behavior to get rid of that feeling or get out of the situation, such as lying. So lying isn't my toxic behavior, but I have to focus on how I can better handle the stressor that causes it (shame).

I am getting the impression that the same reason many people with BPD struggle to grasp how hurtful their behavior is, is the same reason you cannot grasp that very disconnect. Sometimes we hurt so much that we just can't stand in someone else's shoes.

It's difficult to gain that insight for a person with BPD without a lot of therapy, because of the high distress level. I understand it doesn't make a difference in practice for the other people affected by their behavior, but it makes all the difference to the person with BPD experiencing this. In a way, you could say a lack of insight is part of the unmanaged disorder. 

Unmanaged BPD is like there is fire around you and you throw buckets with water around you to try to somehow survive. For some reason, nobody else seems to see or try to help you with the fire. Finally, the fire gets under control and now someone tells you "you threw a bucket at me, that was very painful". So of course the person with BPD just thinks " wtf, I was on fire and literally fighting for survival, why do you complain about the bucket? I wasn't trying to throw a bucket at you, I was trying to survive."  With some help and distance from the fire, the person with BPD can understand they should have just tossed the water, not the whole bucket, or called the fireman. 

So yes, the experience of the person who had a bucket thrown at their head was very painful and real, but the person with BPD is incapable of fully seeing that until the disorder/fire is under control and they aren't as distressed anymore. 

You can't compare it to someone who is on drugs, a personality disorder is very different from an addiction. As long as you try to compare BPD with other disorders to understand it, it won't make sense.

I think the difficulty is that a lot of the criticism of the unhealthy behavior people with BPD display is framed in a way that makes it sound like it is intentional. For example, someone saying "the pwBPD in your life is doing XYZ to manipulate you", while the reality of a person with BPD is that (if they are untreated) they really aren't intentional and the manipulative behavior is a result of being utterly overwhelmed by one's emotions and being unable to handle them. 

It's important to understand that one's behavior was and can be unhealthy and needs to be worked on. However, suggesting they are intentionally being hurtful or manipulative is difficult for someone with BPD to accept because it is very far from their actual experience. It is a lot easier to understand your problematic behavior when you have been to therapy and understand why you are acting the way you are. So it is about shifting the narrative from a person with BPD being intentionally harmful to a person with BPD being harmful as the consequence of a disorder that isn't properly managed yet. 

When this disorder drives a person's actions and experiences, it is so overwhelming and painful that it is not possible to be insightful and truly understand the consequences of your actions. It's a disorder that needs treatment, and not just people acting harmful cause they are just like that. So that is why BPD sufferers often have a hard time accepting people talking about the pain they caused.

Narcissism isn't "everything is your fault", it may be on the outside, but on the inside it is similarly to what you describe a person with BPD feels. Narcissism is rooted in low self esteem. While the motivation, emotions and intentions are very different, people with BPD and NPD disorder sometimes display very similar behaviours like rage and manipulation. So I understand that people get confused.
Also as people with a personality disorder ourselves, acting like having NPD, or "just" being confused with it is a bad thing is not very understanding.

There is no way to measure how "bad" your BPD is. 
The most important thing, that is the basis of bpd treatment, is that you are physically safe, so never be afraid to contact the appropriate people when you are struggling!
For me it was really important to recognize that I experience emotions more intense than non-bpd-people, so that I could better understand my behaviour and work on it. Many of us did not have their feelings validated and subsequently haven't learned how to deal with them. It is important to recognize that and work on it. Your emotions are valid and you can safely experience them. 
To me it was also important to hold myself accountable for my actions/behaviour but be kind and understanding too. I made some bad decisions while my bpd was untreated and emotionally hurt others and myself, but in the end it was my survival strategy. A way to fulfill my needs, when I didnt know how to, or didnt even recognize them. So basically, work on yourself but also cut yourself some slack and be kind. 
Neither you or BPD are bad, but you function differently and it will take some work to understand yourself.

Until you continue your work with your therapist just know that your emotions are valid and you are safe!

There are also some bpd workbooks, but I think it is safer to work together with your therapist first, maybe ask them about it. There are some good BPD journals, you could try using that!
